title: Closest Prime Numbers in Range
statement:
Consider all pairs of prime numbers `num1` and `num2` with `left <= num1 < num2 <= right`. Find the pair whose difference `num2 - num1` is as small as possible and return it as `[num1, num2]`. When several pairs share that smallest difference, return the one with the smaller `num1`.

If the range holds fewer than two primes, return `[-1, -1]`.
notes:
## Intuition

The closest pair of primes in a range is always two *consecutive* primes of that range: any pair with a prime between them is further apart than one of the smaller pairs. So once we know which numbers are prime, one scan over the range comparing each prime with the previous one is enough. Testing each number by trial division would also work but costs O(n·√n); the sieve of Eratosthenes marks every number up to `right` in O(n log log n).

## Approach

1. Build `composite`, a flag per number up to `right`, marking 0 and 1.
2. For each `p` with `p * p <= right` that is still unmarked (so prime), mark every `multiple` from `p * p` upward.
3. Scan `num` from `left` to `right`, skipping composites, and remember the `previous` prime.
4. When a prime `num` follows `previous` with a strictly smaller gap than `answer`, set `answer = [previous, num]`. The strict comparison keeps the earliest pair on ties.
5. Return `answer`, which stays `[-1, -1]` if fewer than two primes were found.

## Example 1, step by step

`left = 10`, `right = 19`. The sieve marks multiples of 2 and 3, leaving 11, 13, 17 and 19 as primes in the range.

- `num = 11`: first prime, `previous = 11`.
- `num = 13`: gap 2, `answer = [11, 13]`, `previous = 13`.
- `num = 17`: gap 4 is not smaller; `previous = 17`.
- `num = 19`: gap 2 ties but is not strictly smaller, so `answer` stays `[11, 13]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(right · log log right) for the sieve plus O(right - left) for the scan.
- Space: O(right) for the flags.

## Pitfalls

- 1 is not prime; mark it (and 0) before scanning, or `left = 1` returns wrong pairs.
- Use `<`, not `<=`, when comparing gaps, so ties keep the smaller `num1`.
- Start the scan at `left`, not 2: primes below `left` do not count.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `composite` | 1 for numbers known not to be prime |
| `p`, `multiple` | the sieving prime and the multiples it crosses out |
| `num` | number being scanned in `[left, right]` |
| `previous` | last prime seen in the range, or `-1` |
| `answer` | closest pair found so far |

narration.2: One flag per number up to right; 1 will mean not prime.
narration.5: Only primes up to the square root of right are needed to cross out every composite.
narration.6: An unmarked p has no smaller divisor, so it is prime.
narration.7: Cross out p's multiples, starting at p * p since smaller ones were crossed out already.
narration.13: No prime seen in the range yet.
narration.14: Scan the range from left to right.
narration.15: Composite numbers cannot be part of a pair.
narration.18: With a previous prime, check whether this gap beats the best one; strict < keeps the earlier pair on ties.
narration.21: This prime becomes the previous one for the next comparison.
narration.23: Return the closest pair, or [-1, -1] if fewer than two primes were found.
